passage: By the third week in the girls' hostel, Disha no longer said she liked sleeping at eleven. At one in the morning the common room was full of instant noodles and a debate about whether the warden was a tyrant. Nirmala was the loudest, and everyone agreed. Disha nodded along, though she thought the warden had been fair over the water shortage. Two girls, Kavya and Sonal, drifted off to bed, and nobody remarked on it. Disha yawned into her sleeve, said "True, true," and stayed until three. In the mirror next morning, someone she barely knew looked back, with the hostel's opinions and her own dark circles.

qa.q: What were the girls debating in the common room?
qa.a: The girls were debating whether the warden was a tyrant.

qa.q: Why did Disha say "True, true" when she thought the warden had been fair?
qa.a: Disha wanted to fit in with the group and did not want to be the odd one; the barely known face in the mirror suggests a faint unease about losing herself.

qa.q: What small choice could Disha make the next night to keep both belonging and her own view?
qa.a: Disha could go to bed at her usual time like Kavya and Sonal did, and say one honest, mild sentence about the water shortage.

qa.q: How might Kavya or Sonal have seen leaving early for bed?
qa.a: Kavya and Sonal seem to have gone without needing an explanation, so leaving quietly may have felt fine to them; it shows the norm had a little room.

grounding: A new college student drifts into hostel habits of late nights and shared opinions, with the peer group becoming a mirror for identity.

passage: Dear Salma, the hostel here is bigger than our whole street. I have started staying up till two with the second-year girls in the corridor, which I never did at home. Last Saturday some of them slipped out for drinks. I said no the first time, but now I say "maybe next week" because saying no again feels like a wall. I laugh at jokes about people from our town that I would not have laughed at before. You once told me I always know what I think. Now I check the corridor first. I am not unhappy, just curious who I am becoming. Write soon. — Farida

qa.q: Until what time has Farida been staying up in the corridor?
qa.a: Farida has been staying up till two with the second-year girls in the corridor.

qa.q: Why does Farida say "maybe next week" instead of no again?
qa.a: Saying no again feels like a wall, so Farida is worried about being left out; the mix of curiosity and unease shows in the closing lines.

qa.q: What could Farida do next to check whether these new habits are really wanted?
qa.a: Farida could pause before answering the next invitation, write down what Farida actually wants, and talk it over with Salma or a trusted adult.

qa.q: What might Salma be thinking when reading that Farida now checks the corridor first?
qa.a: Salma may feel concerned and fond, since Salma once told Farida "I always know what I think", and might reply with a gentle check-in rather than a scolding.

grounding: A new hostel resident drifts into late nights and the group's habits, with the peer group becoming the main mirror away from family.

passage:
You asked what changed in first year? Okay, I'm Anirban, second year now, and I can see it clearly only looking back.
Week one at the hostel, I slept at eleven like at home. By week three I was up at three with the whole wing, eating instant noodles and ranking professors. Mehak, from the next wing, would say, “Prof Iyer is useless,” and I'd say it too, though I'd never sat in her class.
Home felt far. The wing became my mirror. When I went back for Pujo holidays, my mother asked what I thought about something and I actually didn't know. I only knew what the wing thought. That scared me a bit.

qa.q: What did the wing eat at three in the morning?
qa.a: They ate instant noodles.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel when the question from home had no answer?
qa.a: Anirban felt unsettled and a bit scared, realising that only the wing's views came to mind, not Anirban's own.

qa.q: What could Anirban try in second year?
qa.a: Anirban could form a personal view before repeating the wing's opinions, for example by attending a class before judging the professor.

qa.q: How might Anirban's mother have seen the change during the holidays?
qa.a: She may have been puzzled or concerned to find Anirban unsure of any personal opinion after a few months away.

grounding: A student recalls drifting into hostel late nights and shared opinions, where the peer group became the main mirror away from family.

passage:
First week, August: Himani drank water at the hostel's welcome party while her wingmates cheered with beer. She said, “Not my thing,” and went to bed at ten.
Mid-September: She was up past two most nights. The wing had opinions on everything, which canteen dish was trash, which seniors were fake, and she found herself nodding along. Once she had a sip of beer to stop the teasing, and didn't like it.
Late October: Chaitanya, her school friend, called. After ten minutes he said, “You sound like someone else. Since when do you hate the library?” Himani laughed, then stopped. After the call she sat on her bed, trying to remember what she actually thought.

qa.q: What did Himani drink at the welcome party?
qa.a: She drank water.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling after Chaitanya's call?
qa.a: She felt confused and uneasy, sitting on her bed trying to remember what she actually thought.

qa.q: What small step could help Himani find her own view again?
qa.a: She could keep a few of her own habits, like a library hour or earlier nights, and spend time with people outside the wing.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya see Himani on the call?
qa.a: He notices she has changed and sounds like someone else, and he's puzzled and a little concerned.

grounding: Shows a new college student drifting into hostel late nights, a drink and shared opinions, with the peer group becoming her mirror.

passage:
So you're off to hostel next week, Nazia? Let me tell you how it was for your Vidya maasi.
In my first college hostel, my floor did not drink at all. Very strict girls. I didn't drink either, but I also began saying things they said, that the arts students were lazy, that one teacher was a snob. I'd never met the arts students.
By Diwali I came home and argued with my own father, using their sentences. Your nani looked at me and said, “Who is talking, you or your floor?”
I went back and actually sat with the arts students one lunch. They were loud, kind and had better notes. After that I listened to my floor and then decided for myself.

qa.q: What did the floor say about the arts students?
qa.a: They said the arts students were lazy.

qa.q: How might young Vidya have felt when Nani asked her question?
qa.a: She probably felt startled and a bit embarrassed, realising she had been repeating her floor's views as her own.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped young Vidya?
qa.a: Choosing to sit with the arts students at lunch let her test the floor's opinion herself, so she began deciding for herself.

qa.q: How might the arts students have seen Vidya's lunch visit?
qa.a: They seemed welcoming; they were loud and kind and shared better notes, so they probably enjoyed a new face.

grounding: An elder recalls how, away from family, her hostel floor's habits and opinions became her mirror until she began judging for herself.

passage: Baljeet arrived at the Pune hostel in the middle of the monsoon, knowing nobody, with a phone that barely held a charge and his family three states away. By the second week he was up till three every night, because that's when Wing C came alive: card games, loud debates, instant noodles on a smuggled heater. The seniors drank on Saturdays, and Baljeet, who had never touched alcohol, held a glass he didn't drink so he'd fit in. He began repeating their opinions on everything from cricket to politics. Mid-term exams were ten days away. One night his roommate Omkar, who went to bed at eleven, said, 'You don't even like cards.' Baljeet laughed it off, but lying awake later, he couldn't remember the last opinion he'd had that was really his.

qa.q: Until what time was Baljeet up every night?
qa.a: Till three.

qa.q: What did Baljeet feel lying awake at the end?
qa.a: Uneasy and a bit lost, unable to remember the last opinion that was truly his.

qa.q: What could Baljeet try to find himself again?
qa.a: Set a bedtime before the exams, keep one or two of his own habits, and spend time with people like Omkar who notice who he really is.

qa.q: How might Omkar see Baljeet's first weeks?
qa.a: Omkar seems to notice Baljeet changing to fit Wing C and is quietly concerned, pointing out he doesn't even like cards.

grounding: Away from family, a new hostel student drifts into the group's late nights, drinking habits and opinions, and loses track of himself.
